metadata.title: Teacher wellbeing in rural, regional, and metropolitan schools: Examining resources and demands across locations

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Australian 2018 TALIS Teacher Questionnaire data (OECD, 2019) and applies teacher weight values to account for participation probability arising from a two-stage random sample procedure. In the analysis, teacher data are treated as nested in schools using Mplus’ 'complex' command, which adjusts standard errors for the clustered sampling structure. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name in the provided text, but it explicitly states that teacher weights were used. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is described, and the modeling approach is multigroup CFA/SEM rather than ML prediction.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not predict cognitive achievement scores with TALIS plausible values; instead, it models latent constructs (self-efficacy, strain, job satisfaction) using multigroup CFA/SEM. Plausible values are therefore not applicable because the dependent variables are non-achievement, questionnaire-based latent factors rather than PV-based test scores. For missing data, the authors use Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML), which is treated here as multiple-imputation-style handling per the provided mapping.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses the Australian dataset from TALIS 2018. From the original TALIS dataset, cases were excluded when school data were missing the location variable required for multigroup analysis (n=197 excluded). The final analytic sample comprises 3376 schoolteachers from 219 schools who taught students in ISCED level 2 (lower high school years). The OECD’s TALIS sampling exclusions for very remote and very small schools (geographically remote schools, schools with fewer than four students, and geographically remote and small schools) were applied at the population stage, meaning the rural group in this study does not include the most remote/smallest schools. Missing data were handled using FIML in Mplus rather than listwise deletion.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multigroup SEM (M1) explained 27% (rural), 49% (regional), and 30% (metropolitan) of variance in self-efficacy (R2). Standardized path coefficients (b) reported; key effects include: student behavior stress predicted lower self-efficacy in all groups (large effects; e.g., rural b=-0.36***, regional b=-0.54***, metropolitan b=-0.26***). Workload stress predicted greater self-efficacy in regional and metropolitan but not rural; teacher collaboration predicted greater self-efficacy in regional and metropolitan but not rural; pedagogical autonomy predicted greater self-efficacy in rural and metropolitan but not regional. Additional analysis (Teacher strain (latent factor)): Multigroup SEM (M1) explained 49% (rural), 67% (regional), and 45% (metropolitan) of variance in strain (R2). Workload stress and student behavior stress predicted greater strain in all groups (large effects; e.g., student behavior stress b=0.59***/0.34***/0.34*** across self-efficacy/strain/job satisfaction paths as reported in Table 6). PD-needs did not predict strain in any group. PD-irrelevance predicted greater strain only for rural teachers (moderate effect; b=0.14*/0.00/0.02 pattern with rural significant). Teacher collaboration predicted lower strain for regional and metropolitan but not rural; pedagogical autonomy did not predict strain; self-efficacy predicted greater strain across all groups (small-to-moderate effects). Two rural interactions were retained: PD-needs * teacher collaboration (DR2=0.03) and PD-irrelevance * teacher collaboration (DR2=0.04), with collaboration buffering PD-irrelevance for strain in rural teachers. Additional analysis (Teacher job satisfaction (latent factor)): Multigroup SEM (M1) explained 30% (rural), 42% (regional), and 51% (metropolitan) of variance in job satisfaction (R2). Student behavior stress predicted lower job satisfaction in all groups (moderate-to-large effects; e.g., rural b=-0.36**, regional b=-0.26*, metropolitan b=-0.21*). Workload stress predicted lower job satisfaction for regional and metropolitan but not rural. PD-needs did not predict job satisfaction in any group. PD-irrelevance predicted lower job satisfaction for rural and metropolitan but not regional. Teacher collaboration predicted higher job satisfaction for all groups, while pedagogical autonomy predicted higher job satisfaction for regional and metropolitan but not rural; self-efficacy did not predict job satisfaction in any group.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 Australia (ISCED 2) Teacher Questionnaire the study leveraged student behavior stress, PD-needs, PD-irrelevance, teacher collaboration, and pedagogical autonomy to predict teacher self-efficacy, finding that student behavior stress was the only consistent (negative) predictor across rural, regional, and metropolitan groups while several demands/resources showed location-specific salience (e.g., collaboration mattered for regional/metropolitan but not rural; pedagogical autonomy mattered for rural/metropolitan but not regional). This indicates that rural teacher self-efficacy may be most effectively supported through interventions targeting student behavior management and strengthening teachers’ pedagogical autonomy, rather than relying on collaboration or PD-needs alone.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 Australia (ISCED 2) Teacher Questionnaire data to examine how job demands/resources and personal resources relate to teacher self-efficacy, strain, and job satisfaction across rural, regional, and metropolitan school locations. The authors fit multigroup CFA/SEM models in Mplus (complex command for nested teachers-in-schools) and use teacher weights to account for the two-stage sampling design. Missing data were handled with Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML). The multigroup SEM (M1) explained 27–49% of self-efficacy variance, 42–67% of strain variance, and 31–51% of job satisfaction variance, with student behavior stress emerging as the only consistent predictor across all outcomes and locations. The paper is cross-sectional, so associations cannot be interpreted causally, and the modeling is not ML-based prediction (no PVs are involved).
